props.title: Groove

sections.content: Groove (2000) captures the underground rave scene at its millennial peak, diving into San Francisco's electronic music culture with documentary-like authenticity. Director Greg Harrison, drawing from his own experience in the scene, crafts a night-in-the-life story that stands alongside other vital dance culture films like Human Traffic (1999) and Go (1999). What sets Groove apart is its loving attention to the details that made raves magical: the secret locations, paper flyers, elaborate preparation, and transformative power of communal dance experiences. The film's technical accuracy about DJ culture and electronic music production remains impressive, avoiding the clichés that plague many EDM-focused movies.

sections.content: The late 90s/early 2000s saw a wave of films attempting to capture club culture authenticity. While Party Monster (2003) focused on the outrageous excess, and It's All Gone Pete Tong (2004) explored the darker side of DJ fame, Groove took a more grounded approach. The film's strength lies in showing how raves created temporary autonomous zones where people could forge genuine connections. This theme resonates with earlier countercultural films like Dazed and Confused (1993), though with distinctly millennial energy and optimism.

Harrison's direction demonstrates deep respect for rave culture's rituals and unwritten rules. The film features actual DJs like John Digweed and forest psytrance pioneer Dmitri playing themselves, lending credibility other dance music films lack. The attention to detail extends to the accurate portrayal of vinyl mixing techniques, proper sound system setup, and the intricate logistics of throwing underground parties. This technical accuracy makes Groove an important document of a specific moment in American dance music history. SUBHEAD: Impact on Dance Music Cinema

sections.content: Groove influenced later electronic music films like We Are Your Friends (2015) and Beats (2019), though few matched its cultural authenticity. The film stands as a time capsule of pre-9/11 optimism, when the underground rave scene still felt like a revolutionary movement rather than a commercial enterprise. Its loving portrayal of PLUR (Peace Love Unity Respect) culture contrasts sharply with modern EDM festival films that focus more on spectacle than community.
